content: The midwife was responsible for conducting regular check-ups, providing consultations, assisting in the creation of birth plans, and offering parental education. They collaborated with obstetricians and other healthcare professionals as needed. The midwife was on call for the woman’s labor and delivery, except in specific circumstances. Each woman had the opportunity to receive continuous one-to-one care from the onset of labor until two hours postpartum. A psycho-educational intervention was implemented to prevent and treat postpartum depression. This included mailing educational manuals to participants, face-to-face counseling sessions, and psychological counseling via telephone tailored to individual risk factors. The mailed materials provided information on the pathogenesis, risk factors, and prevention of postpartum depression, based on domestic and international research. They also included Q&A sections addressing social support, marital relationships, and child-rearing responsibilities. Face-to-face counseling involved weekly appointments at a maternal and child health hospital, with each session lasting at least 40 minutes. Telephone counseling was available for those unable to attend in person, with a designated hotline managed by a trained individual. Women with severe postpartum depression symptoms, despite these interventions, were referred to psychiatric specialists for further treatment. A participatory antenatal education program was conducted, covering topics such as anatomical and physiological changes during pregnancy, nutrition, common complications, mental health, communication skills, delivery methods, pain management, and postpartum health. Emphasis was placed on components of health locus of control (HLC), including internal HLC, powerful others HLC, and chance HLC. Training materials were distributed, and workshops were held for both women and their spouses. Mothers were placed in a supine position during complementary medicine interventions, with room temperature maintained at 26°C. A trained nurse facilitated skin-to-skin contact between the mother and infant, known as kangaroo care, for 30 minutes. Some participants were exposed to soft instrumental music, such as Johann Sebastian Bach’s relaxation compositions, played through headphones during the session. Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) programs were designed to enhance happiness through structured sessions. Techniques included increasing physical activity, improving planning and organization, fostering creativity, enhancing social connections, and promoting intimacy. Sessions also addressed depression, postpartum symptoms, and coping strategies. Homework assignments were given to practice learned skills, and post-tests were conducted to evaluate progress. Psycho-educational interventions included group sessions, structured pharmacotherapy when necessary, and systematic monitoring of clinical progress. Topics covered symptoms, treatments, problem-solving, and behavioral activation strategies, with examples relevant to the postnatal period. Medical appointments were scheduled regularly to ensure treatment adherence, and cost-free pharmacotherapy protocols were available for women requiring medication. Participatory learning and action cycles involved community discussions, case studies, and the implementation of strategies to address maternal and newborn health problems. Psycho-social stimulation programs adapted from the Jamaican home visiting model were delivered through weekly home visits. These visits used low-cost toys and materials to improve maternal-child interactions and support developmentally appropriate learning activities. Breastfeeding training emphasized the benefits of breast milk for both mother and infant, as well as techniques for expressing and storing milk. One-on-one training sessions lasted at least one hour, and mothers received informational booklets. Educational programs used items from the Neonatal Behavioral Assessment Schedule to help mothers understand their infant’s unique capacities and sensitivities. Printed materials and short films demonstrated parenting practices, such as showing love, avoiding harsh discipline, and engaging in responsive feeding and play. Community health staff conducted weekly home visits to facilitate age-appropriate play activities and discuss child nutrition, parenting challenges, and discipline strategies.
